hypothesis: If Darwin is right, fossil occurrences in the Paleobiology Database are overwhelmingly of taxa with mineralized hard parts, and soft-bodied taxa appear only as rare exceptions.
pass_criterion: Using PBDB occurrences, the claim is supported if (a) at least 90% of marine animal genera have a mineralized skeleton (composition field: carbonate, silica, phosphate or similar) and at most 10% are non-mineralized or soft-bodied, AND (b) at most 5% of collections are flagged as having soft-part preservation, and wholly soft-bodied phyla such as Nemertea and Platyhelminthes account for under 1% of all occurrences.
fail_criterion: The claim is refuted if soft-bodied or non-mineralized genera exceed 25% of marine animal genera, or if more than 15% of collections record soft-part preservation, or if wholly soft-bodied phyla account for 5% or more of occurrences.
interpretation: Darwin's 'wholly soft' organisms are read as taxa with no mineralized or decay-resistant tissue, measured through the PBDB taxon 'composition' and 'taphonomy' fields and through phylum-level counts. Darwin's 'not preserved' is read as 'preserved only rarely', because Burgess Shale-type Lagerstätten show that soft tissue can be preserved under exceptional conditions. The second half of the claim, that remains left on non-depositing sea floor disappear, is not tested directly. It is tested only indirectly, through the overall hard-part bias. The 'strongly biased' conclusion is read as the heavy skew toward hard-part taxa. This is a modern reinterpretation: it tests the generalization as a strong statistical bias, not as an absolute prohibition.

dataset.name: The Paleobiology Database
dataset.why_it_fits: PBDB gives fossil collection and occurrence records with taxon composition and taphonomy fields. It has a public data API and a download generator. Fields used: taxon phylum and genus, composition, and the collection taphonomy and soft-part preservation fields. I did not check the exact field names against the API documentation, so they must be confirmed before analysis.
